By net EPA the two teams are close (-0.094 vs -0.112) and their point differentials are nearly identical (-6.3 vs -7.0 per game). Laying a touchdown on the road against a division rival is a lot for a team that is 0-4 against the spread. Tennessee's run-heavy, clock-shortening style also works against margin.

Titans games average about 34.6 combined points (13.8 scored, 20.8 allowed), and Tennessee is last in pass rate over expected. Houston's non-elite opponents scored 20 and 19, and the Texans' own run game can't drain clock efficiently either way. The main risk is Stroud hitting deep shots against a Titans secondary that ranks 31st in deep EPA.

The teams grade nearly identically by net EPA (-0.087 vs -0.069). Indy brings a roughly 4.6-EPA-per-game special-teams edge, far fewer penalties, and a run game that fits Pittsburgh's 29th-ranked tackling and Harmon's absence. The turnover matchup against PIT's 6th-ranked takeaway defense is the main risk.

Both passing offenses rank near the bottom (30th and 27th by EPA), and the Colts lean on a clock-controlling run game. Indy's 25.5 points a game outrun its 26th-ranked yardage. Pittsburgh's 27th-ranked deep defense is the main threat to the under, and Indy is short on the receivers to exploit it.

Philadelphia scores 18.8 per game with a full roster and ranks 29th in offensive EPA. It is now missing Smith, Goedert, Brown and Lane Johnson, with Jurgens and Barkley uncertain. Jacksonville allows 13.3 points and opponents score touchdowns on just 28.6% of red-zone trips.

The net EPA gap is extreme (2nd vs. 31st), Jacksonville has covered three of four, Philadelphia has covered none, and the injury report tilts heavily one way. It's only a lean because 7 is a key number and Philadelphia's 4th-ranked special teams can produce a backdoor cover.

Three of Jacksonville's four games went under, with combined scoring averaging about 39 points. A shorthanded Eagles offense plus a Jaguars game plan built on the run and clock control points the same way. The risk is Jacksonville's defense giving up chunk plays, which keeps this from being a stronger play.

bets.market: KC spread vs. LAC (line not yet posted)
bets.reason: Kansas City is rested off a bye and ranks 3rd in net EPA against a 29th-ranked Chargers team. The Chargers have the 31st special teams unit and are missing much of their offensive line. Kansas City has failed to cover only as a favorite in shootouts with better offenses, and LAC's offense is 31st.
The Chargers average 16.8 points with the 31st-ranked offense and a run game that ranks 25th. They now face Kansas City's 8th-ranked run defense with Slater out and Alt questionable.
Kansas City averages one sack per game. LAC has allowed 12 sacks in four games (3 per game), ranks last in hit rate allowed, and is likely starting backups at tackle.

The Rams have the better net EPA (0.104 vs 0.078) and play at home. Buffalo is 75% ATS with positive wins over expected while the Rams' turnover luck has been among the worst in the league. Buffalo's corner injuries hit exactly where Stafford can attack.

Buffalo ranks 28th in pass EPA allowed and 27th in explosive passes allowed and is without its 91%-snap corner. The Rams' line has allowed pressure at the fourth-lowest rate, so Buffalo's 8th-ranked rush is less of a threat.

Denver is laying more than a field goal on the road with a -5 point differential per game, a 2-0 record in one-score games and the league's worst run defense facing a run-first opponent. The Chargers' defense ranks 12 spots better by EPA, and Surtain is doubtful. The Chargers' line injuries keep this a lean rather than a strong play.

Denver averages 18.5 points (26th) and 282.8 yards (27th). It faces a defense that ranks 11th in EPA allowed and 2nd in takeaways, and it is missing receiver Pat Bryant and running back Jonah Coleman. The risk is the Chargers' offense handing Denver short fields with turnovers again.

Las Vegas is 5th in net EPA with a +7.8 point differential, while New England is 16th and -3.0 per game, yet the Raiders are getting more than a field goal. The Patriots are also missing their top corner and a starting DT. Expect some regression from the 4-0 ATS run, but the number still looks a half-point too generous.

The spread and total imply about 24.5 points for a Patriots offense averaging 16.3 (30th). That offense faces the 2nd-ranked pressure defense and the league's takeaway leader, and is short its top receivers. The Raiders' red-zone leakiness is the main risk.

+160 implies roughly a 38% win chance for the team with the better efficiency profile, protection and pass rush in this matchup. The weak NE offense and its turnover problems make an outright upset more plausible than the price suggests.

The spread and total imply Miami scores about 17.75, but it has not topped 13 in any game. Cincinnati brings the second-best sack rate and the third-stingiest red-zone defense against an offense ranked 31st in success rate.

Three of Miami's four games went under, and its offense supplies so little that Cincinnati would need to score close to 30 on its own. The risk is Burrow against a pass defense ranked 29th, which keeps this a lean rather than a like.

The net EPA gap is about 0.3 per play, and Miami lost three of four by 14 or more while covering only once. Cincinnati's receiver and secondary injuries, with Chase and Higgins both questionable, are the reason this isn't stronger. Confirm Chase's status before betting it.

Minnesota ranks seventh in net EPA to the Saints' 17th, and its top-ranked pass rush meets a line that ranks 24th in pressure allowed. The Saints are also -1.3 per game in turnovers against a +1.3 defense. The injuries justify a short line, but the defensive mismatch looks larger than a point and a half.

Three of four Minnesota games went under, and the offense has averaged about 15.7 points outside its Week 1 outlier. That was before losing Jefferson, a starting guard and possibly the left tackle. Saints games have run high, but the Saints' offense hasn't faced a defense allowing 12.8 per game and the league's lowest red-zone TD rate.

The spread and total imply roughly 22 points for Minnesota, a number its 31st-ranked yardage offense has reached once. The Saints' last-ranked run defense is a real opening, but a battered line and no Jefferson make a slow, field-goal-heavy game the likelier script.

By EPA Las Vegas is the better team (5th in net EPA to New England's 16th), with the 2nd-ranked defense, yet it is getting more than a field goal. That spread looks like it prices in last year's Patriots. The caution is that the Raiders' 3-1 includes +1.42 wins over expected and a 4-0 cover streak, so some of their record is luck too.

Laying nearly 2-to-1 means betting on an offense that ranks 30th in scoring and has two-plus giveaways every week, against the league leader in takeaways and a top-two pressure defense. The Patriots' secondary is also missing Gonzalez against a top-seven passing offense. The price assumes the old version of this team.

The spread and total imply about 24.5 points for New England. The Patriots have topped that once in four games, and that was against the 29th-ranked defense. Las Vegas allows 21 per game with a defense ranked 2nd in EPA, though its 29th-ranked red-zone defense is the risk to this under.

The Saints' implied 20.5 points sits well below their 27-per-game pace, which is fair against a defense allowing 12.8 a game and leading the league in pressure. Minnesota's offense is last in success rate and 31st in yards, and it is now without Jefferson and a starting guard. The risk is Saints giveaways handing over short fields, which is why this is only a lean.

Season-long net EPA has these teams within 0.013 of each other, and the Giants hold a roughly 9-point-per-game special teams edge over a Washington unit ranked 28th. Washington is also missing McLaurin, Cosmi, Cross and White, with Daniels coming off a dislocated elbow. The lean strengthens if Daniels is limited or doesn't start, and weakens if he's fully cleared.

Cleveland's 3-1 rests on a perfect one-score record and the 2nd-most wins over expected, despite a -3.5 point differential. The two teams are near-equal by efficiency, and the Browns are missing both interior offensive linemen. The Jets' own injuries keep this a lean rather than a strong play.

Three of the Jets' four games have gone under. Both lines give up sacks at bottom-eight rates, and both teams rank bottom-five in penalties, all of which kill drives. The Jets are also missing their lead back, a top receiver and a tight end.

The record suggests a good team, but Cleveland ranks 21st in point differential and 15th in net EPA while committing the most penalties in the league. Their luck in close games is the kind that regresses.

The net EPA gap is enormous (2nd vs 31st), and the Eagles are 0-4 ATS even when healthy. Their best receiver, tight end, both tackles and possibly their center are now out. Jacksonville's run game and quick passing attack target exactly what this defense does worst.

The spread and total imply about 17.75 points for Philadelphia, close to its 18.8 average. That average came with a healthier lineup, and the offense ranks 30th in success rate. Jacksonville takes the ball away and is stingy in the red zone, so the under is the lean, tempered by Jacksonville's deep-ball leaks and the likely regression of its red-zone numbers.

Pittsburgh is at home on 10 days' rest, and the matchups line up in its favor. The Colts' 28th-ranked pressure rate loses Key against the Steelers' main weakness, and Indy's -1.5 turnover margin meets a top-six takeaway defense. The Colts' 75% cover rate is propped up by second-ranked special teams, which tends to be the least repeatable edge.

Indianapolis allows 393 yards per game (31st) and 26 points per game. Pittsburgh's offense scored 30 and 24 in its last two games, and it should face the lightest pass rush it has seen. Combined with a likely short field or two from Colts turnovers, the Steelers clearing their implied number is the more likely side.

Both teams allow fewer than 19 points a game, and Seattle's run-heavy approach shortens games. The total is higher than any of Seattle's four lines this year (40.5 to 44.5). Blending each offense's scoring with the other defense's points allowed lands closer to 45 than 47.5.

San Francisco's net EPA of 0.267 is more than double Seattle's 0.122, yet the market prices this as a road field goal. Seattle's offense ranks 26th in rushing EPA, is down its top two backs and has had Lock under center for three weeks, which limits its ability to take advantage of San Francisco's injuries. Kept to a lean because the 49ers' numbers came mostly against weak defenses and Bosa and Sigle are out.

All four Tampa losses came by seven or fewer points behind a defense ranked 5th in EPA. Dallas pairs an elite offense with the 31st-ranked defense, which has forced only 2 takeaways. The roughly 0.10 per-play net EPA gap plus home field supports something closer to a touchdown than 9.5. The short week, backup quarterback and missing secondary starters keep this a lean rather than a strong play.

These are near-identical teams: point differential per game is -7.0 vs. -6.3 and net EPA is -0.112 vs. -0.094. Yet Houston is laying a full touchdown on the road while 0-4 against the spread and missing its top linebacker. Tennessee lost by 4 and 6 when getting 7 or more against Philadelphia and Baltimore.

At +275 the price implies roughly a 27% chance, which is low for a home team whose efficiency is close to its opponent's. Tennessee's league-worst special teams and weak passing game keep this a small play rather than a strong one.

Washington rates better than New York in net EPA (19th vs 22nd) and plays at home. The Giants' 3-1 comes with a perfect one-score record and +1.33 wins over expectation, a profile that typically regresses. The Giants' 9-plus EPA special-teams edge and Washington's QB uncertainty keep this from being stronger.

Both defenses rank bottom-five at keeping red-zone trips to field goals (80% and 75% TD rates), and the Giants allow 48.9% on third down, which extends drives. Washington's games have averaged 52.5 total points with three of four going over. The Giants' run-heavy, clock-eating style is the main thing pulling the total down.

Washington's 6th-ranked pressure rate has produced only 7 sacks in four games. The Giants allow sacks on 8.7% of dropbacks, 27th, and have taken 11 already, so this is the spot for pressure to convert.
